title: Self-Paced Module: Complete GUI Application
continues: Week 20 — Market Analysis and a System Proposal

objectives.cognitive: Link a limited set of requirements and a user flow to the Week 20 own-theme proposal.
objectives.affective: Make realistic promises and distinguish existing, planned, completed and unverified work.
objectives.psychomotor: Draw an interface plan and write needs-linked requirements and checks for one useful task.

blocks.markdown: Work offline in order with the printed module, JDK and existing sources. Keep each public class in its named .java file in one folder. Compile javac *.java; java Main opens Vehicle; java RequestDemo opens school-materials practice. Use your own launcher for assessed work.

Use the complete Week 20 starting files directly: they already include all four Week 19 steps. Do not reapply old steps. Vehicle: java Main, with the Week 18 launcher/readiness group and Week 19 JComboBox TerminalPanel. School-materials practice: java RequestDemo, with Preview, Info, Rename and confirmed Clear. Keep LayoutDemo, ThemeLayoutCheck, all other optional demonstrations, every .txt backup, the Vehicle model and exceptions, FareService/FareCheck, ReadyTask and DispatchThread, BoardingTask, ReadyReport, ConvoyLeg and LoadingBay. InvalidDistanceException extends RuntimeException directly; keep its separate catch.

Course history: Week 11 classes/objects; 12 four OOP pillars; 13 exceptions; 14 collections; 15 file handling; 16 threads; 17 Swing basics; 18 layouts/panels; 19 advanced components/user interaction; 20 market analysis/system proposal.

A GUI (graphical user interface) uses windows and controls to work with a program. A complete classroom application finishes one useful user task, checks input and explains its limits. A requirement is a behavior you can check; a user flow is the path from starting an action to a useful result [YS].
A school desk needs a clear path from choosing materials to a readable draft. More counters do not help if nobody can finish the request.

**Continue your proposal.** Name your own theme, users and problem. Reuse Week 20 findings and label assumptions. Existing means already in the program; planned means proposed; completed means built with stated checks; unverified means not yet checked. A completed feature may still have unverified usability.

**Worked example and justified revision.** Keep the school-materials draft. Week 20 planned local save/load, but did not build it. Defer that feature to protect time for safe integration and menus; retain the current one-session preview task. The hypothetical scenario, costs, benefits and estimates were not field research. No new survey is required.

rows: R1: choose subject, at least one material and collection place; Preview gives a summary or a correctable error.
R2: Rename accepts 1–30 trimmed characters; Cancel keeps the name. Clear changes choices only after explicit Yes.
R3: Request has Preview/Rename/Clear; View has Info. Each menu uses the same behavior as its button.

blocks.markdown: **Worked flow:** open → select subject/materials/place → Preview → read summary. On an error, correct the choice and Preview again. Rename is optional. Clear offers Yes/No/Cancel; closing its dialog also keeps choices. Preview is a snapshot: after editing choices, Preview again.

**Activity 1 | Own-theme design.** In your notebook, name your existing capability, user/task/problem and proposal link. Write 3–5 limited requirements with a need and a concrete check each. Draw nested panels and a menu plan; mark inputs, action, model method and result. Write the normal flow, correction path and cancellation path. Justify a reduced scope using Week 20 feasibility.

**Boundary:** the example does not submit, reserve stock, save/load or serve simultaneous users. Closing the window loses its draft. Use invented request labels, not personal data. Your own task must remain useful within its stated limits.

rows: Name the theme, user and task.
Write R1–R5 as needed, with a need and concrete check each.
Name the revision and justify it.

blocks.markdown: **Daily allocation:** 10 min recall + 20 min scope + 20 min worked design + 40 min own plan + 20 min review/slip + 10 min revision = 120 min.
1. Yale University [YD]. [Discovery](https://usability.yale.edu/ux/discovery). Excerpt: “real goals”. Identify the intended users and their task.
2. Yale University [YS]. [Define the Scope](https://usability.yale.edu/ux/plan/define-the-scope). Excerpt: “success criteria”. Limit requirements to needs and available resources.

3. Yale University [YT]. [User Testing](https://usability.yale.edu/ux/validate/review-the-user-experience/user-testing). Excerpt: “complete tasks”. Observe task attempts and record problems before revision.

4. Massachusetts Institute of Technology [MIT]. [Graphical User Interfaces](https://ocw.mit.edu/ans7870/6/6.005/s16/classes/24-graphical-user-interfaces/index.html). Excerpt: “view tree”. Separate interface actions from application rules; nest views.

5. University of Pennsylvania [PA]. [Design and Usability Testing](https://accessibility.web-resources.upenn.edu/testing-evaluating-accessibility/design-and-usability-testing). Excerpt: “visible labels”. Use visible labels, clear actions and keyboard alternatives.
**Key validated facts:** Choose a user task and realistic boundaries [YD] [YS]; connect controls to application rules [MIT].

blocks.markdown: Connecting controls, layouts, existing model rules and feedback so one user can finish a task. Nested panels are panels inside other panels; a layout arranges their controls. A model holds application data or rules; a listener is code called when an action occurs [MIT] [N1].
A materials desk connects its form, checking rule and readable result. A separate attractive form with no working route to the rule leaves the task unfinished.

**Trace the retained RequestDemo.** It already combines the controls and rules below. Today reuse that complete workflow and explain its structure; no replacement of the worked example is needed. Build or repair the equivalent connection in your own theme program.

rows: choices NORTH; result CENTER; actions SOUTH.
subject label NORTH; scrollable JList CENTER; options SOUTH.
materials row and collection-place row, each using FlowLayout.
Preview/Info call summary(); it checks required choices. Rename uses acceptName(); Clear uses clearIfConfirmed().

blocks.markdown: **Follow an action:** button → actionPerformed() → summary() → useful text or IllegalArgumentException caught as feedback. This retained teaching example keeps request rules in methods of the same class. In your own theme, call the existing model method; do not duplicate its calculation in a listener. Vehicle already routes TerminalPanel through FareService to Vehicle.quoteFare(). Do not merge the two programs.

**Read existing code, not a replacement:** `result.setText(text);` displays the current summary; `summary()` throws if a required choice is missing. Keep those checks. A disabled or empty choice is not a reason to remove validation.

**Actual direct-check results:** with no subject: IllegalArgumentException: Choose a subject. With Java but no material: IllegalArgumentException: Choose materials. Java + Guide + Desk returns: Java: Guide=true; Sheet=false; Place=Desk. These came from method checks on the event dispatch thread, not live clicks. Headless means using no display: that launcher run showed no window.

**Safe interface work.** The event dispatch thread (EDT) handles Swing events and interface updates [KS]. Keep short checks there. Slow work runs outside listeners; return updates through SwingUtilities.invokeLater(). Retain Main’s ReadyTask and Week 16 helpers. This draft preview has no slow operation, so it needs no new worker or storage.

**Activity 2 | Own-theme workflow.** Combine existing components and useful nested panels. Trace one action to its model method and visible result. Compile locally with javac *.java; run your own launcher. Record normal input, missing/invalid input, correction and cancellation. State expected and actual results separately. Back up each working file before changing it.

**Check yourself:** can a classmate complete the task from labels alone? Does invalid input preserve editable choices? At minimum and larger window sizes, can all controls still be reached? Keep the interface’s result and your description consistent.
Connection record: control → listener → model method → result. Nested groups: parent/layout contains child/layout. Record any repair or remaining check.
**Draw and check the own-theme workflow.** Sketch labelled input, nested panels, action, model method and feedback. Add the correction and cancellation routes. Keep this with your test record.
**Daily allocation:** 10 min recall + 20 min integration trace + 20 min worked checks + 45 min own workflow + 15 min partner check + 10 min slip = 120 min.

objectives.cognitive: Explain JMenuBar, JMenu and JMenuItem and trace a menu action to existing behavior.

blocks.markdown: JMenuBar is the menu strip, JMenu groups related choices, and JMenuItem is an action inside a menu. Its listener works like a button listener [N2].
Request and View are like labelled desk folders. Inside each folder, each instruction performs a real task rather than merely showing a decorative label.

**Step 1 | Add menus to the worked example.** First copy the previous working RequestDemo.java to RequestDemo_week20.txt. Keep every earlier backup. Then replace RequestDemo.java with the complete listing below. Do not run half a file. No other existing file changes. Compile javac *.java; run java RequestDemo.

**What changes:** createMenuBar() adds Request → Preview/Rename/Clear and View → Info, using the same listener as the retained buttons. The frame installs that bar. Subject/material/place keyboard mnemonics and a scrollable result improve access. Existing validation, dialogs and safe confirmation remain. A mnemonic is a letter used to navigate controls; an accelerator runs an action directly: Ctrl+P previews [N2].

blocks.markdown: **Activity 3 | Own-theme menus.** Back up working sources. Add a menu bar with clearly named menus and only purposeful items linked to your existing actions/model. Choose distinct navigation letters. Record normal, invalid, corrected, declined and cancelled outcomes. Never treat “not No” as permission to destroy data. Use an explicit Yes test.

**Check yourself:** selecting a menu without adding a listener cannot perform the task. Reusing the same handler avoids different rules for buttons and menus. The example’s Clear keeps the request name; explain exactly what your own destructive action resets.

**Read the safety rules in the listing:** acceptName(null) returns without changing the name; invalid text leaves the name unchanged. clearIfConfirmed() alone authorizes clearing after Yes. Closing Info changes no request fields. These direct method outcomes were tested; a real dialog still needs the school-computer checks.
Own menu trace: item → command → model/rule → feedback.

lessons.title: Complete and Repair Your Own Application

blocks.markdown: A comparison between each promised behavior and what an actual trial showed. Compilation checks syntax and types; it cannot prove that a person can finish the task [YS] [YT].
Before calling a desk ready, compare each promise on its sign with what a user can actually complete.

**Activity 4 | Complete your own-theme performance task.** Use your Week 20 proposal and Monday plan. Finish one useful workflow, menus, checks, correction and safe cancellation. Use the performance-task tools below. Run the school-computer checks below, record failures, repair the responsible code once, then repeat the failed test and one surrounding successful test. Keep useful workers; do not introduce slow work into listeners.

**Test record format:** requirement ID | input/action | expected | actual | pass/fail/unverified | repair | retest. Record what happened, including messages; never copy an expected result into the actual column without running it. Classmate role-play is classroom feedback, not field research.

columns: Record actual result; do not pre-mark Pass
rows: Open your launcher; complete the normal task by buttons and every menu item. Confirm the model result.
Use Tab/Shift+Tab and arrows/Space; try menu letters (example Alt+R/Alt+V), item letters and Ctrl+P. OS shortcuts can differ.
Check the example at 520×380 and larger; verify labels, controls and scrolling remain reachable. Test your own minimum size.
Info opens/closes; Rename Cancel/close, blank, 31 characters, valid trim; Clear No, Cancel and close all keep choices; only Yes clears.
Make invalid input, correct it and repeat. Edit after Preview, then preview again; compare summary with current choices.
While Vehicle Check ready is running, move/resize the window and use controls; repeated clicks stay disabled until completion. Check your own workers if used.

performanceTask.title: Own-theme Complete GUI Application
performanceTask.markdown:
Start Thursday; complete and present Friday. Build a modest application using your own existing theme and Week 20 proposal, with justified revisions. Complete one useful task. Submit sources/backups, design, needs-linked requirements, actual test/repair records, checklist and short user notes. No database, networking, account, paid tool, external library or new storage feature is required.

**Starter with blanks**

My existing theme is ____; users ____ need to ____ because ____. My proposal planned ____; I kept/revised ____ because ____. Requirements R1–R__ and needs: ____. Interface groups/layouts: ____. Flow: start ____ → action ____ → model ____ → result ____. Error/cancel path: ____. Menus/items/keys: ____. Retained worker (if needed): ____. Tests and actual results: ____. Repair/retest: ____. Existing ____; built and checked ____; planned/deferred ____; still unverified ____.

**Self-check**

- One useful task matches proposal/revision? Yes / Not yet
- Model, controls and menus agree? Yes / Not yet
- Errors correctable; cancel safe; Yes explicit? Yes / Not yet
- Keyboard, resize and worker checks recorded? Yes / Not yet
- Every requirement has actual evidence or an unverified label? Yes / Not yet
- Limits, repairs and documentation honest? Yes / Not yet

**Planning record**

User/task; requirement → need → check; panel/layout; normal/error/cancel flow.

**Requirements versus results**

For every requirement: ID | input/action | expected | actual | status | repair | retest. Use pass/fail/unverified honestly.

**Two three-hour days**

Thursday: 10 min recall + 15 min requirements review + 90 min completion + 35 min test/repair + 15 min notes + 15 min slip = 180 min. Friday: 10 min recall + 30 min consistency/usability + 25 min repairs + 20 min documentation + 20 min rehearsal + 60 min presentations + 15 min slip = 180 min.

Large class: circles of at most 12 allow 12 × 5 min = 60 min. Peer listeners keep evidence notes; the teacher rotates and reviews every application and record.

**Scoring**

Full points: complete and evidenced; about half: partly working or weak evidence; zero: absent/unrelated. Award intermediate whole points. Do not reward extra controls or feature count. The task score includes presentation; slip scores are separate.
